analysis.one_liner: Extends key foreign surveillance powers three weeks and forces release of a secret surveillance court ruling.
analysis.headline: Introduced the day the warrantless surveillance authority was set to expire, the bill would stretch it to May 21, 2026 and require public release of a secret surveillance court opinion by May 12; it has no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: Section 702 of the FISA Amendments Act lets the government collect the communications of foreign targets without a warrant, a program that sweeps in many Americans' calls and emails. This bill would extend that authority for just three weeks instead of the longer renewal the intelligence committees have pursued — and it would require the Director of National Intelligence to publicly release a secret surveillance court ruling about the program from March 17, 2026, with redactions only to protect sources and methods. In practice, the short extension plus the disclosure deadline makes the release of the secret opinion the price of continuing the program.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose communications get collected under Section 702, mostly incidentally and without any individual warrant. They gain a public accounting of what the surveillance court found about the program — something Congress and the public would otherwise debate without seeing. The bill's sponsor frames the three-week extension as a way to keep the program from lapsing while that disclosure happens first.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Director of National Intelligence, consulting the Attorney General, to publicly release the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court's March 17, 2026 opinion and order on Section 702 certifications by May 12, 2026, redacting only what is needed to protect sources and methods.

Extends the legal authority for Section 702 from April 30, 2026 to May 21, 2026, with the change taking effect retroactively if enacted after the original date, so the program does not lapse while the disclosure deadline runs.

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence agencies that have kept the surveillance court's ruling about the program classified would lose that secrecy on a firm deadline. Communications providers that are legally compelled to help the government collect communications would keep carrying that obligation for three more weeks.

drawbacks.text: The bill continues Section 702 unchanged for three more weeks, meaning warrantless collection that sweeps in Americans' communications goes on with no new limits, no warrant requirement for searches of Americans' data, and no other reforms.

The required release permits 'such redactions as may be necessary to protect intelligence sources and methods,' a broad carve-out the intelligence agencies could use to black out substantial parts of the court's reasoning.

A three-week extension is a bridge, not a decision: it defers the real fight over the program's long-term future, and the disclosure deadline may simply be overridden by a longer reauthorization bill that never includes it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure requirement is a genuine transparency win — the public would finally see a court ruling that shapes how a mass surveillance program is run. But the bill buys it by keeping the program running as-is, and the transparency is only as good as the redactions the agencies choose. Its value depends entirely on whether the released opinion actually changes the terms of the long-term reauthorization fight; if a longer bill passes without the disclosure condition, the extension bought nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced the day Section 702's authority was set to expire and sent straight to the Intelligence Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden introduced the bill on April 30, 2026, the day the existing repeal date for Title VII surveillance authorities fell.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Select Committee on Intelligence, which has taken no further action on it.

The bill's two operative parts are a public-release deadline for the court's March 17, 2026 Section 702 opinion and a three-week extension of the surveillance authorities through May 21, 2026, effective retroactively if needed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved: the Intelligence Committee has avoided the forced disclosure of the secret court opinion, and the program's long-term future remains undecided. The agencies' preference for deciding 702's fate without the disclosure condition is intact for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies, for now — no forced disclosure

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator (OR); member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 30, 2026 pairing a three-week extension of Section 702 with a hard deadline to declassify the surveillance court's opinion on the program.

against.name: Tom Cotton
against.role: Chair, Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
against.what_they_did: The committee he chairs has taken no action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: There are no votes and no cosponsors on either side; the only recorded positions are the Democratic sponsor's support and the committee's silence.

industries.note: The bill hands them three more weeks of warrantless collection authority under Section 702, but strips away the secrecy of the surveillance court's March 2026 ruling on the program on a firm deadline. Their interest in operating the program without public disclosure runs against the public's interest in knowing how it is run.

Section 702 legally compels communications providers to help the government collect targeted communications; the extension keeps that compelled-assistance obligation in place. Providers get no choice in the matter either way, and many have previously sought limits or liability protections.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no action in the committee that oversees the program, this bill is unlikely to move on its own. Its realistic role is as a lever in the larger fight over long-term Section 702 reauthorization: either the disclosure condition gets folded into a broader deal, or the committee advances a longer extension without it and this bill dies quietly at the end of the Congress.
